## Today's question

> **Did states that expanded Medicaid in 2014 have lower working-age
> mortality than states that did not?**

## Today's Ballgame

::: incremental
**Explore**: What does mortality look like across states that expanded Medicaid and those that did not?
  &nbsp;&nbsp;→ `plt.hist()`, `.boxplot()`, group means

**Test**: Is the difference in these states bigger than chance would produce?
  &nbsp;&nbsp;→ `stats.ttest_ind()`

**Check**: does the answer to our second question depend on unreasonable assumptions?
  &nbsp;&nbsp;→ permutation test

**Extend**: how can we formally express and model these differences?
  &nbsp;&nbsp;→ `smf.ols("rate ~ expanded")`
:::

## How today works

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| **Module 1** | I do | I drive. You type every line with me. |
| **Module 2** | We do | Pairs. Most of the code is given; you write the four that matter. |
| **Module 3** | You do | On your own. Nine steps, no code. |

The analysis is the *same shape* all three times. That is deliberate, because by
the third pass, the shape is yours.

# Module 1: I do

## Two things to name first

Every line today is built from two kinds of thing: **objects** and **functions**.

::: incremental
- An **object** is something you made and gave a name to. It sits in the
  Variables pane until you overwrite it or restart Python.
- A **function** does something. You give it a name, a pair of parentheses,
  and whatever it needs to know inside them.
:::

## Step 1: load the tools

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
```

Python on its own does not know about tables, plots, or statistics. Those
live in **libraries**, and you load the ones you need at the top of every
script.

::: fragment
`import pandas as pd` loads pandas under a short nickname: `pd.` means
*the pandas version of*. Everyone uses these same five nicknames.
:::

## Anatomy of a function call

::: {.anatomy .big}
[pd.]{.fragment .highlight-current-red fragment-index=1}[read_csv]{.fragment .highlight-current-red fragment-index=2}[(]{.fragment .highlight-current-red fragment-index=3}[\"data/medicaid.csv\"]{.fragment .highlight-current-red fragment-index=4}[,&nbsp;]{.fragment .highlight-current-red fragment-index=6}[index_col=0]{.fragment .highlight-current-red fragment-index=5}[)]{.fragment .highlight-current-red fragment-index=3}
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
**`pd.`** says where the function lives: in pandas, the table library,
which we just loaded under the short name `pd`.
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
**`read_csv`** is the function name. It says what you want done.
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}
**`( )`** holds everything the function needs to know.
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=4}
**`"data/medicaid.csv"`** is the first argument: which file to read.
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=5}
**`index_col=0`** is a named argument: treat the first column as row
labels, not data. (Python counts from 0, so column 0 *is* the first.)
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=6}
**`,`** separates one argument from the next.
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=7}
Two questions get you through any function: **what do I want Python to
do**, and **what does Python need to know to do it?**
:::

## Step 2: read the data

```{python}
counties = pd.read_csv("data/medicaid.csv", index_col=0)
```

Nothing printed. That is what success looks like: `=` stores silently.

::: fragment
Look at the **Variables** pane. `counties` is now in it.
:::

## Step 2: three questions

```{python}
counties.shape
```

```{python}
counties.columns
```

```{python}
counties.head(3)
```

Ask these of every new dataset: **how big, what columns, what's a row.**

::: fragment
The dot means *belonging to*: `counties.shape` is the shape of `counties`.
With parentheses, `.head(3)` **does** something; it is a *method*.
Without them, `.shape` just **looks something up**; it is an *attribute*.
:::

## Step 3: look at the outcome

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.5
plt.figure()
plt.hist(counties["crude_rate_20_64"])
plt.show()
```

Never test a variable you have not looked at. Defaults are fine; we are not
decorating anything yet.

::: fragment
`plt.figure()` starts a fresh picture and `plt.show()` shows it. Skip
`plt.figure()` and your next plot lands on top of this one.
:::

## What are those `[" "]`?

::: {style="font-size: 1.3em; text-align: center; margin: 0.6em 0;"}
`plt.hist(counties`[`["`]{.pop}`crude_rate_20_64`[`"]`]{.pop}`)`
:::

You have not seen square brackets used like that before. **Don't look it up yet.**

::: fragment
Use what is already on the screen:
:::

::: incremental
- `counties` is the table you just read in
- `"crude_rate_20_64"` was in the list `.columns` printed
- so `[" "]` has to pick **one of its columns** out of **a table**
:::

::: fragment
**Use the context clues.** Read around the unfamiliar piece first, guess
what it has to be, then check. Faster than looking it up cold, and it
sticks.
:::

## Reading from the inside out

`plt.hist(counties["crude_rate_20_64"])` has two steps, and the inner one
happens first.

::: incremental
1. `counties["crude_rate_20_64"]` pulls the column out. On its own it is a
   Series: one number per county.
2. `plt.hist()` draws that Series.
:::

::: fragment
> "Take the `crude_rate_20_64` column out of `counties`, and draw a
> histogram of it."
:::

## Step 4: get the data ready

> **Did states that expanded Medicaid in 2014 have lower working-age
> mortality than states that did not?**

What do we need to do to our data before we can answer that?

::: fragment
**1. Aggregate.** Expansion is a *state* policy, so we need one
mortality rate per state, for 2014.
:::

::: fragment
**2. Deal with the NAs.** How is the policy recorded right now?

```{python}
counties["yaca"].head()
```

`yaca` is the year a state expanded; `NaN` (missing) means never. We need
a clean 1 or 0.
:::

::: fragment
**3. Weight by population.** The smallest and largest counties in 2014:

```{python}
#| echo: false
d2014 = counties[counties["year"] == 2014]
limits = d2014["population_20_64"].agg(["min", "max"])   # 224 and 6,298,815
ends = d2014[d2014["population_20_64"].isin(limits)].sort_values("population_20_64")
deaths = ends["crude_rate_20_64"] * ends["population_20_64"] / 1e5
pd.DataFrame({"people aged 20-64": ends["population_20_64"].map("{:,}".format),
              "deaths": deaths.round().astype(int).map("{:,}".format),
              "% who died": (deaths / ends["population_20_64"] * 100).map("{:.3f}%".format)}
             ).set_axis(ends["county"])
```

Averaging county rates gives these two the same vote. **Is that a
reasonable comparison?**
:::

::: {.notes}
Take answers for each before revealing the next. On 3: one death in
Arthur County would put it at 0.446%, nearly twice Los Angeles. The three names are the
plan for the next several slides: aggregate, deal with the NAs, weight by
population. We take them in the order the code needs them: keep 2014,
label the states, then add up deaths and people by state.
:::

## Step 4a: keep one year

```{python}
d2014 = counties[counties["year"] == 2014]
d2014.shape
```

::: fragment
Square brackets with a `True`/`False` test inside keep the rows where the
test is `True`. `==` asks *is this equal to?*: a question, so it is
doubled.
:::

## Reading a line, right to left

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; text-align: center; margin: 0.5em 0;"}
`d2014 = counties[counties["year"] == 2014]`
:::

Longer lines are still one sentence. Start at the right:

::: incremental
- `counties[counties["year"] == 2014]` says *from `counties`, keep the rows
  where `year` is 2014* …
- `=` says *… and store it* …
- `d2014` says *… as `d2014`.*
:::

::: fragment
> "**From `counties`, keep the rows where `year` is 2014, and store that
> as `d2014`.**"
:::

::: fragment
If you can say a line out loud, you understand it. If you cannot, stop
and ask.
:::

## Step 4b: label each state

```{python}
d2014["expanded"] = np.where(d2014["yaca"].notna() & (d2014["yaca"] == 2014), 1, 0)
d2014["expanded"].value_counts()
```

`np.where(test, value_if_true, value_if_false)` runs down the whole column.

::: fragment
Note the square brackets doing a second job: on the **left** of `=` they
create a column rather than pulling one out.
:::

## Why the `.notna()` guard

A missing value answers `False` to *every* comparison, so `NaN == 2014`
quietly lands in the 0 group. The guard says so out loud: *not missing,
and equal to 2014.*

::: fragment
The trap: Python does `&` **before** `==`. Drop the parentheses and there
is no error:

```{python}
np.where(d2014["yaca"].notna() & d2014["yaca"] == 2014, 1, 0).sum()
```

Every county lands in "did not expand". Silent wrong answers are worse
than errors.
:::

## Ask Python itself

```python
help(pd.Series.mean)
```

The **Help** pane lists every argument and its default:
`Series.mean(*, axis=0, skipna=True, ...)`. So pandas skips missing values
unless you say otherwise.

::: fragment
```{python}
counties["median_income"].mean()
counties["median_income"].mean(skipna=False)
```

Fifteen rows are missing an income, and the first answer left them out
without a word. When a result looks off, `help()` the function and check
its defaults.
:::

::: {.notes}
Before the fragment, ask the room: how many arguments does `.mean()` take,
what does `skipna` do (scroll to Parameters), and what is it set to if you
don't say? `.isna().sum()` counts what was skipped.
:::

## The template: *y* broken down by *x*

One pattern does most of the work today.

::: {style="font-size: 1.5em; text-align: center; margin: 0.5em 0;"}
`data.groupby(x)[y].goal()`
:::

Read `groupby(x)`, `by=x`, and `~ x` as **"broken down by"**.

| | |
|---|---|
| `states.groupby("expanded")["rate"].mean()` | group means |
| `states.boxplot(column="rate", by="expanded")` | a picture |
| `smf.ols("rate ~ expanded", data=states)` | a model |

The t-test is the odd one out: it wants the two groups handed over one at
a time.

## Step 4c: weight by population

A rate is deaths over people. To get a state's rate, turn each county's
rate back into deaths, add up the deaths and the people by state, and
divide once.

```{python}
d2014["deaths"] = d2014["crude_rate_20_64"] * d2014["population_20_64"] / 1e5

states = d2014.groupby(["state", "expanded"],
                       as_index=False)[["deaths", "population_20_64"]].sum()
states["crude_rate_20_64"] = states["deaths"] / states["population_20_64"] * 1e5
states = states.sort_values("state")
states.shape
```

::: fragment
The template again: `d2014.groupby(x)[y].sum()`, where *x* is state and
expansion status and *y* is deaths and population. Two of each, so both go
in a **list**, `[ ]`.
:::

::: fragment
Sorting changes nothing today, but the shuffling in step 7 depends on row
order. Make the order a decision you can see.
:::

::: {.notes}
`as_index=False` keeps state and expanded as ordinary columns, so we get a
plain table. Leave the parentheses off `.sum` and Python prints
`<bound method ...>` instead of an answer.
:::

## DESCRIBE · Step 5: look at the comparison

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4
states.boxplot(column="crude_rate_20_64", by="expanded")
plt.show()
```

```{python}
states.groupby("expanded")["crude_rate_20_64"].mean()
```

`.boxplot()` starts its own fresh picture, so no `plt.figure()` this time.

## DESCRIBE · Step 5: the estimate, as one number

```{python}
group_means = states.groupby("expanded")["crude_rate_20_64"].mean()
diff_obs = group_means[1] - group_means[0]
diff_obs
```

Expansion states averaged about **39 fewer deaths per 100,000**
working-age people.

Is that more than luck would hand us?

::: fragment
`group_means[1]` is the row *labelled* 1: the expanded states.
`np.float64(...)` is numpy saying what *kind* of number this is. The number
is the part inside.
:::

## TEST · Step 6: the test you already know

```{python}
result = stats.ttest_ind(states["crude_rate_20_64"][states["expanded"] == 1],
                         states["crude_rate_20_64"][states["expanded"] == 0],
                         equal_var=False)
result
result.confidence_interval()
```

Read all of it. The **interval** tells you the size of the gap the data
supports. The p-value never does.

::: fragment
`equal_var=False` asks for Welch's t-test, which does not assume the two
groups are equally spread out.
:::

## Which way round?

We computed `diff_obs = −39`. The interval says **−91 to +12**. Same sign.

::: fragment
`ttest_ind(a, b)` subtracts **a − b**, and we handed it the expanded
states first: **group 1 − group 0**, the same way round as `diff_obs`.
:::

::: fragment
Swap them and every sign flips, with no warning. When a sign looks wrong,
check which way round the subtraction went.
:::

## CHECK · Step 7: what does p = 0.13 actually mean?

Most of us walk in carrying this one:

> ~~"p is the probability the result is due to chance."~~

::: fragment
It has the logic **backwards**.
:::

::: fragment
It **assumes chance is all there is**, and then asks:

> if expansion made no difference at all, how often would luck alone hand
> us a gap as big as ours?
:::

## CHECK · Step 7: so let's build one

::: incremental
- The null hypothesis says the labels are meaningless.
- So let's *make* them meaningless by shuffling which states expanded.
- Do that a thousand times, and we have a thousand worlds where the policy
  did nothing.
- Then just count how many of them beat our real result.
:::

::: fragment
We don't have to trust a formula for this. **We can just do it.**
:::

## Step 7: one fake world

```{python}
rng = np.random.default_rng()
shuffled = rng.permutation(states["expanded"])

(states["crude_rate_20_64"][shuffled == 1].mean() -
 states["crude_rate_20_64"][shuffled == 0].mean())
```

`rng` is a random number generator: the thing that does the shuffling.
Run it again:

```{python}
shuffled = rng.permutation(states["expanded"])
(states["crude_rate_20_64"][shuffled == 1].mean() -
 states["crude_rate_20_64"][shuffled == 0].mean())
```

That bouncing **is** sampling variation. You are looking straight at it.

## Step 7: a thousand fake worlds

```{python}
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
diffs = []
for i in range(1000):
    shuffled = rng.permutation(states["expanded"])
    diffs.append(states["crude_rate_20_64"][shuffled == 1].mean() -
                 states["crude_rate_20_64"][shuffled == 0].mean())
diffs = np.array(diffs)
```

The seed, `2026`, makes the shuffling repeatable. `for i in range(1000):`
runs the indented lines 1000 times; `.append()` keeps each answer. The
indent *is* the grouping, so line it up exactly.

## Step 7: and there it is

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.2
plt.figure()
plt.hist(diffs)
plt.axvline(diff_obs, color="red", linewidth=2)
plt.show()
```

```{python}
(abs(diffs) >= abs(diff_obs)).mean()
```

A p-value you built out of shuffling and counting.

::: fragment
The t-test said 0.132. Not identical, and it shouldn't be: 1000 shuffles
is itself a sample. Same conclusion: not distinguishable from chance with
39 states.
:::

## That one line does three things

```python
( abs(diffs) >= abs(diff_obs) ).mean()
```

| | |
|---|---|
| `abs()` | drops the minus sign, so we count both tails: past −39 and past +39. That is what "two-sided" means, and it is what `ttest_ind()` did. |
| `>=` | gives a `True`/`False` for each of the 1000 shuffles |
| `.mean()` | of `True`/`False` gives the proportion that are `True`, because `True` counts as 1 |

::: fragment
Drop the `abs()`:

```{python}
(diffs >= diff_obs).mean()
```

Our difference is negative, so this counts almost every shuffle. No
warning, just a wrong number.
:::

## MODEL · Step 8: the same answer, as a regression

```{python}
m = smf.ols("crude_rate_20_64 ~ expanded", data=states).fit()
print(m.summary())
```

`smf.ols()` sets the model up, outcome `~` predictor. `.fit()` fits it.
`print()` lays the table out.

## MODEL · Step 8: you need two numbers from that

Both on the **`expanded`** row:

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| `coef` | **−39.18** | our difference in means, exactly |
| `P>|t|` | **0.131** | our p-value |

`Intercept`, on the row above, is the mean of the group coded 0: the
baseline. Everything else answers questions we haven't asked.

::: fragment
A difference in means *is* a regression coefficient. t-test, permutation
test, and regression: three ways of asking one question, and they agree.
:::

::: {.notes}
`equal_var=False` is Welch's correction, which is why the t-test's df was
34.63 rather than 37. `equal_var=True` matches `ols()` to the decimal.
:::

## Step 9: why we used 39 rows and not 2,372

```{python}
stats.ttest_ind(d2014["crude_rate_20_64"][d2014["expanded"] == 1],
                d2014["crude_rate_20_64"][d2014["expanded"] == 0],
                equal_var=False).pvalue
```

That is the same test, run on the counties.

::: fragment
`p` is about 6e-17. Overwhelming, and wrong.
:::

::: fragment
It thinks it has 2,372 independent observations. It has 39: every county
in a state shares one policy decision.
:::

::: fragment
When a p-value looks too good, ask how many independent things you
actually measured.
:::

## That was the whole game

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
| Step | What you did | With |
|---|---|---|
| 1–2 | Load tools, read the data | `pd.read_csv()` `.head()` |
| 3 | Look at the outcome | `plt.figure()` `plt.hist()` `plt.show()` |
| 4 | Get the data ready | `np.where()` `.notna()` `.isna()` `.value_counts()` `.groupby()` `.sum()` `.sort_values()` |
| 5 | Describe | `.boxplot()` `.mean()` |
| 6 | Test | `stats.ttest_ind()` `.confidence_interval()` |
| 7 | Check | `np.random.default_rng()` `.permutation()` `range()` `.append()` `np.array()` `plt.axvline()` `abs()` |
| 8 | Model | `smf.ols()` `.fit()` `.summary()` `print()` |
| Module 2 | Split at the median | `.median()` |
:::

Twenty-eight functions and methods: a difference in means, a permutation
test, and a regression, plus the reason to distrust one of them.

## Glossary: the twenty-eight functions and methods

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {style="font-size: 0.52em;"}
**Get data, look at it**

| | |
|---|---|
| `pd.read_csv()` | read a spreadsheet off disk |
| `.head()` | show the first few rows |

**Pictures**

| | |
|---|---|
| `plt.figure()` | start a fresh, blank picture |
| `plt.hist()` | distribution of one variable |
| `.boxplot()` | compare groups |
| `plt.axvline()` | add a vertical line to the picture |
| `plt.show()` | show the picture |

**Build a grouping variable**

| | |
|---|---|
| `np.where()` | test each value, return 1 or 0 |
| `.notna()` / `.isna()` | is this value present / missing? |
| `.value_counts()` | count how many in each category |

**Summarise**

| | |
|---|---|
| `.groupby()` | split a table by group; what follows runs on each |
| `.mean()` | average, and on True/False a proportion |
| `.sum()` | add up |
| `.median()` | the middle value |
| `abs()` | drop the minus sign |
| `.sort_values()` | sort the rows by a column |
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {style="font-size: 0.52em;"}
**Test and model**

| | |
|---|---|
| `stats.ttest_ind()` | compare two group means |
| `.confidence_interval()` | the interval for that difference |
| `smf.ols()` | set up a linear model, `y ~ x` |
| `.fit()` | fit it |
| `.summary()` | the model's coefficient table |
| `print()` | lay that table out properly |

**The permutation test**

| | |
|---|---|
| `np.random.default_rng()` | a random number generator; give it a seed to repeat it |
| `.permutation()` | shuffle into a random order |
| `range()` | the numbers 0 to n − 1, for a loop to count through |
| `.append()` | add an answer to the end of a list |
| `np.array()` | turn a list into an array, so maths works on all of it |

**Look something up** (attributes: no parentheses)

| | |
|---|---|
| `.shape` | how many rows and columns |
| `.columns` | what are the columns called |
| `.pvalue` | just the p-value from a test |
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.72em; margin-top: 0.5em;"}
Three more appear only in the finish-early extensions: `plt.scatter()`,
`plt.axline()`, and the `.params` attribute. And `help()` works on all of
them.
:::
:::

::::

## Glossary: the symbols

::: {style="font-size: 0.6em;"}
| | | |
|---|---|---|
| `#` | everything after it is ignored | `# this is a note` |
| `import … as` | load a library under a nickname | `import pandas as pd` |
| `=` | store this as | `x = 5` |
| `=` | name an argument, *inside* a function | `data=states` |
| `()` | run a function; what it needs goes inside | `abs(x)` |
| `,` | separates one argument from the next | `plt.hist(x, bins=20)` |
| `.` | belonging to: a library's function, an object's method or attribute | `pd.read_csv`, `states.shape` |
| `" "` | a string: text, taken as-is | `"data/medicaid.csv"` |
| `[" "]` | pull one column out of a DataFrame | `states["expanded"]` |
| `~` | "broken down by", inside a model formula | `"rate ~ expanded"` |
| `==` | *is* equal to: a question, not an instruction | `year == 2014` |
| `>=` `<=` `>` `<` | the usual comparisons | `diffs >= 64` |
| `&` | and; put each side in its own `( )` | `x.notna() & (x == 2014)` |
| `:` + indent | the indented lines below belong together | inside the `for` loop |
:::

::: fragment
`=` does both jobs, and you will see both. Python's style guide writes the
first with spaces (`x = 5`) and the second without (`index_col=0`). It makes
the two jobs visible.
:::

## Glossary: square brackets do four jobs

The one that catches everyone. Same symbol, four different meanings:

::: {style="font-size: 0.74em;"}
| | | |
|---|---|---|
| `df["col"]` | pull one **column** out of a table | `counties["year"]` |
| `df[test]` | keep the **rows** where a test is True, in a table or a single column | `counties[counties["year"] == 2014]` |
| `s[label]` | pick one value by its **label** | `group_means[1]` |
| `["a", "b"]` | make a **list**; inside `df[ ]` it picks several columns | `[["deaths", "population_20_64"]]` |
:::

::: fragment
If you get a `KeyError`, read the last line of the message: it names what
pandas could not find. It is almost always a column name spelled wrong.
:::

## What's new in Module 2

Two things you have not seen:

**Making groups from a number.** Poverty is continuous, so you split it
at the median with `np.where()`.

**A result that runs off the page.** Your red line may sit far out past
the whole null distribution. That empty space *is* the result, not a
drawing glitch.

::: fragment
If the p-value line gives you `0`, that is not p = 0. None of 1000
shuffles got that far, so **report p < 0.001**.
:::

## Two rules for your own work

**Always open the folder.** Never write `os.chdir("/Users/you/...")`. It
works on exactly one computer, and not for long. Open the project folder
and every path in your script stays relative.

**Never use `%reset` to start clean.** It deletes your variables, but
libraries stay loaded and any settings you changed stay changed. It does
not give you a clean session. Restart Python instead: **Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+0**.

::: fragment
If a script only runs after you have run some *other* thing first, it isn't
finished.
:::

# Appendix

## Inside the quotes: a path

::: {.anatomy .big}
[\"]{.fragment .highlight-current-red fragment-index=1}[data/]{.fragment .highlight-current-red fragment-index=2}[medicaid[.csv]{.fragment .highlight-current-red fragment-index=4}]{.fragment .highlight-current-red fragment-index=3}[\"]{.fragment .highlight-current-red fragment-index=1}
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
**`" "`** make it a **string**: text, taken as-is. Without them, Python
reads `medicaid` as the name of an object, goes looking, and fails.
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
**`data/`** is a folder. Folder, slash, file: that is a **path**,
directions to the file, starting from the folder you opened.
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}
**`medicaid.csv`** is the file itself.
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=4}
**`.csv`** is the **extension**: what kind of file it is. Comma-separated
values, a table saved as plain text. `pd.read_csv()` reads this kind; an
Excel `.xlsx` needs a different function. Finder and File Explorer hide
extensions by default, so you may only see `medicaid` there.
:::

## Mac vs. Windows

The full path to the same file, on two laptops:

| | |
|---|---|
| **Mac** | `/Users/you/intro-to-python/data/medicaid.csv` |
| **Windows** | `C:\Users\you\intro-to-python\data\medicaid.csv` |

::: incremental
- Ours skips all of that. `data/medicaid.csv` starts from the folder you
  opened, so it is the same on every laptop.
- In Python, always write `/`, even on Windows. A lone `\` can silently
  turn into a special character: in `"data\new.csv"`, the `\n` becomes a
  line break, and Python goes looking for a file that does not exist.
  `/` never does that.
:::

## Set up Python, once

For anyone who arrives without a working setup. These go in the
**Terminal** (**Terminal → New Terminal**), not your script. Copy them from
the README; don't retype them.

1. Install **uv**, the tool that sets up Python for you:

   Mac:

   ```bash
   curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
   ```

   Windows:

   ```powershell
   powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"
   ```

2. Close that terminal (the trash-can icon) and open a new one, so it can
   find uv.
3. Run `uv sync`.
4. Pick the `.venv` Python in the top-right corner, then run
   `scripts/00-check.py` (**Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+Enter**). It should end with
   `You're ready.`

`uv sync` builds a `.venv` folder holding pandas, numpy, scipy,
statsmodels, and matplotlib, in the versions this workshop was tested
with. It downloads Python 3.12 for it if you need one. Already have a
different Python, like 3.14? That's fine: uv leaves it alone.
